L.p: *-er* /ə/ is used for the person who does an activity: writer, painter, shopper. It is sometimes written *-or*: actor, donor, operator, sailor, supervisor. *-er*/*-or* are also used for things that do a job: pencil sharpener, bottle opener, projector, stapler. *-ee* /iː/ is the person who receives the action: employer → employee, payer → payee.

Noun suffixes: *-er/-or* for people or tools (*donor*, *supervisor*, *sharpener*, *stapler*); *-ee* for the person something is done to (*employee*, *payee*); *-ism* for activities and beliefs (*journalism*, *tourism*); *-ist* for people with a belief or skill (*pianist*, *journalist*); *-ness* for states (*readiness*, *kindness*).
The suffixes *-able* and *-ible* mean 'that can be done': *washable* (can be washed), *edible* (safe to eat), *flexible* (can bend easily, or can change).
*-ise* (often *-ize* in American English) turns adjectives and nouns into verbs: *modern* → *modernise*, *computer* → *computerise*, *global* → *globalise*.

L.p: Prefixes give adjectives a negative or opposite meaning: fair → unfair, experienced → inexperienced, similar → dissimilar. L.tip: *In-* does not always make a word negative; it can mean 'inside' or 'into': internal, import, insert, income.

L.p: *Un-* and *dis-* reverse the action of a verb: tie → untie, appear → disappear, agree → disagree, approve → disapprove, connect → disconnect, prove → disprove, qualify → disqualify, do → undo, fold → unfold, load → unload, lock → unlock, veil → unveil, wrap → unwrap, zip → unzip.

L.h: A Verbs based on Latin roots

L.p: Many English words are formed from Latin roots, and they often sound fairly formal. Knowing the root helps you guess the meaning.

t: conduct, induce (also: viaduct, a high bridge)

L.e: A famous conductor will conduct the choir tonight. The match was postponed because of heavy rain. The government plans to impose a new tax on plastic bags. Mozart composed his first symphony as a child. The bank requires a deposit of £500. He was deported for working without a visa. The judges were impressed by her performance. L.p: *Compound adjectives* are made of two words, usually joined with a hyphen: *bad-tempered*, *good-looking*, *ice-cold*. Often the second part is an *-ed* or *-ing* form, and you can usually work out the meaning from the parts.

L.tip: Write *up-to-date* with hyphens in front of a noun (an up-to-date map), but usually without them after *be*: The map is up to date. Many compounds follow this pattern.

L.e: The witness described the thief as a broad-shouldered, left-handed man in a tight-fitting jacket and brand-new trainers. Her story about him escaping by helicopter sounded rather far-fetched, but her rosy-cheeked son agreed with every word.

L.p: *Absent-minded* = often forgetting things, with your mind elsewhere; *easy-going* = calm and not easily worried or annoyed; *warm-hearted* = kind and generous to others; *quick-witted* = able to think and answer fast; *two-faced* = saying one thing to you and another behind your back; *self-centred* = interested only in yourself; *stuck-up* = behaving as if you're better than others (informal).

L.h: D Compounds with a preposition or particle

L.e: The company made an all-out effort to finish on time. My parents are quite well-off, but as a student I'm always hard-up. After the long walk, my boots were completely worn-out. Fifty years ago this was farmland; now it's a built-up area.

The president travels in a car with bullet-proof windows. We bought the sofa in a cut-price sale with interest-free credit. Don't leave everything to last-minute revision! L.tip: Swap one half of a compound to make new ones: *short-sleeved*, *long-sleeved*; *home-made*, *hand-made*; *open-minded*, *narrow-minded*.

L.p: *Compound nouns* combine two or more words into one noun with a single meaning: *bus stop*, *human being* (a person), *science fiction* (stories set in an imagined world of future science). Some are written as one word (*trademark*), some with a hyphen (*self-control*), and some as two words.

L.h: B How are compound nouns written?

L.p: If you understand both parts, the meaning is usually clear. Most are written as two words (tin opener, bank account, pedestrian crossing), some with a hyphen (self-control) and some as one word (earring, trademark, babysitter). There are no strict rules, and dictionaries vary.

Most compound nouns are stressed on the first part: *BURGlar alarm*, *WINDscreen*, *STEERing wheel*. A few stress the second part: *heart atTACK*, *food POIsoning*. A dictionary will show you the stress.

L.h: A Compound nouns based on phrasal verbs

L.p: Many nouns are formed from phrasal verbs: *break down* → a *breakdown*; *work out* → a *workout* (a session of exercise). The plural adds *-s* at the end: two workouts, several takeovers.

These nouns often sound informal and are very common in newspapers: *walkout* = a strike; *crackdown* = strong action to stop something; *breakout* = an escape; *shake-up* = a big change; *break-up* = the end of a relationship.

L.e: Nurses staged a walkout over pay. Police have announced a crackdown on illegal parking. The singer's break-up with her band shocked fans. The new director promised a shake-up of the whole department.

L.p: *Outlet* = a place to sell products; *check-out* = the cash desk in a shop; *cutback* = a reduction; *turnover* = the money passing through a company; *bailout* = money given to a company to save it from failure.

L.e: The government announced cutbacks in spending on roads. The shop has an annual turnover of two million pounds. The supermarket has opened a new outlet near the station. The queue at the check-out was enormous.

L.p: *Input* = information put in; *output* = production; *staff turnover* = how quickly staff leave and are replaced; *dropout* = a person who rejects society or leaves a course; *fallout* = radioactive dust after a nuclear explosion; *printout* = paper with printed computer information; *breakthrough* = an important discovery.

*Breakdown* = failure; *outlook* = what is likely to happen; *drawback* = a disadvantage; *outcome* = the result; *feedback* = comments; *outset* = the start; *set-up* = an arrangement or situation; *outbreak* = the start of something unpleasant.

L.e: The economic outlook for next year is uncertain. The main drawback of the flat is the noise. From the outset, the team worked well together. The new bypass has taken traffic away from the town centre. There has been an outbreak of flu at the school.

L.p: *Binomials* are pairs of words joined by a conjunction (usually *and*), and their order cannot normally change: we say *peace and quiet*, never *quiet and peace*. Many rhyme or begin with the same sound, which makes them easy to remember. *Odds and ends* are small items of little value; *give and take* means both sides being willing to compromise.

L.x: The order is fixed: we can pack the *odds and ends* (not *ends and odds*) later.

L.e: Long hours are part and parcel of being a doctor. My dad was ranting and raving about the parking ticket. The old mill has gone to rack and ruin. Our teacher was very prim and proper. The campsite was rough and ready, but cheap. The company likes to wine and dine its best customers. The airline cancelled our flight and left us high and dry.

With so many jobs available, graduates can pick and choose. Her piano playing has improved in leaps and bounds. I go to the countryside for some peace and quiet. First and foremost, we need to find a venue.

L.h: C Binomials made of grammar words

L.e: There were a few clouds here and there. It's been raining on and off all day. The dog ran back and forth along the beach. Grandpa is out of hospital and out and about again.

L.tip: Your language probably has binomials too. Check whether similar ones have the same word order in English.

L.h: D Binomials linked by other words

L.h: A Abbreviations said as individual letters

L.tip: In abbreviations spoken as letters, the strongest stress normally goes on the final letter: I got cash from the AT*M*. Please reply AS*AP*.

L.p: When the letters are read as a word, the abbreviation is an *acronym*: *PIN* (personal identification number) rhymes with *win*. *SAD* (seasonal affective disorder) is low mood in the dark winter months; a soldier who is *AWOL* (absent without leave) has left without permission. A few acronyms are now ordinary words, written in lower case: *radar*, *scuba*, *sonar*.

Some words are shortened in informal use: *kilo* (kilogram), *gig* (gigabyte), *air con* (air conditioning), *satnav* (satellite navigation), *uni* (university), *mobile* (mobile phone), *carbs* (carbohydrates), *sci-fi* (science fiction), *high-tech* (high technology).

L.h: A Learning and remembering multi-word expressions

L.p: The meaning of an idiom is often impossible to guess from its words, so learn each one as a single unit, together with its grammar. For example, *have seen better days* (= be old and in poor condition) is used about things and normally in the present perfect: My old bike has seen better days. *Take the weight off your feet* is a friendly invitation to sit down.

These expressions are often informal and add a personal comment, sometimes humorous or ironic. Don't use them just to sound fluent. To someone you don't know in a formal situation, don't say 'Do take the weight off your feet'; say 'Do sit down' or 'Have a seat'.

By grammar: *get the wrong end of the stick* = misunderstand; *pull a fast one* = trick someone; *poke your nose into* = interfere; *be over the moon* = be extremely happy; *be in the red* = owe money to the bank.

By meaning: *as daft as a brush* = very silly; *takes the biscuit* = is the worst of all; *a pain in the neck* = a nuisance; *as good as gold* = very well-behaved. By a key word: *make a meal of* = make something seem more important than it is; *make a move* = leave; *on the make* = wanting money or power for yourself; *make heavy weather of* = make slow progress with.

Some idioms have fixed grammar. *Bark up the wrong tree* (= have the wrong idea about something) nearly always appears in the continuous form: If you think I took your keys, you're barking up the wrong tree.

L.x: I think *you're barking up the wrong tree* (not *you bark up the wrong tree*).

L.tip: In standard British English, *r* is silent unless a vowel follows: card /kɑːd/, park, work, mother /ˈmʌðə/, water. It is pronounced in American, Irish and Scottish English.

L.p: With many two-syllable words that are both noun and verb, the noun has stress on the first syllable and the verb on the second: The workers held a PROtest. / They proTESTed outside the office. The same pattern applies to *record*, *increase*, *import*, *permit* and *present*.

L.p: Countable nouns can be used with *a/an* and made plural: a hat, two hats. Uncountable nouns are not normally used with *a(n)* or in the plural: Can you give me *some information* (not *an information* or *some informations*)? Learn them in groups by subject.

L.p: You can make many uncountable nouns countable with *a piece of* or *a (little) bit of*, and plural with *pieces of* or *bits of*. *Bit* is less formal, suggests a smaller amount, and is used with all kinds of nouns; *piece* is used more with uncountable nouns.

L.p: Collective nouns describe a group of the same people or things: a *group* of people (smaller number), a *crowd* of people (large number), a *gang* of thieves (rather negative).

units.sub: do without, make up for, make a fuss of

L.h: A Phrasal verbs with do and make

L.p: *Do without* = manage without; *do away with* = get rid of; *make for* = move towards; *make of* = think of (an opinion); *make off* = leave in a hurry; *make up for* = compensate for.

L.e: When the power went off, we had to do without hot water for two days. Many schools have done away with uniforms. After the film, we made for the nearest café. What did you make of her speech? The thieves made off with the cash. The beautiful view made up for the long climb.

L.h: B Phrasal verbs with several meanings

L.p: *Do up* can mean fasten, renovate, or wrap into a bundle. *Make out* can mean claim, manage to see, or understand. *Make up* can mean invent, form (be made up of), put on cosmetics, prepare by mixing (a prescription), or make more complete (make up the numbers).

L.h: C Collocations with do and make

L.p: As a rough guide, *do* goes with tasks, jobs and activities (*do the ironing*, *do your best*, *do business with* a firm), while *make* often goes with things we create or cause (*make a cake*, *make a noise*, *make arrangements*, *make an effort*, *make an excuse*). Some *make* phrases describe how we treat people: *make allowances for* someone, *make a fuss of* someone, *make fun of* someone.

L.x: Please *make a decision* (not *do a decision*) by Friday. She *does business* (not *makes business*) with companies in Spain.

L.p: *Bring up* = raise (a child); *bring off* = succeed in something difficult; *bring on* = cause (an illness) to start; *bring about* = cause to happen; *bring out* = introduce (a product); *bring back* = re-introduce; *bring down* = lower, or remove from power; *bring round* = persuade.

L.e: She was brought up by her aunt in Glasgow. Nobody thought he could win, but he brought it off. Cold weather can bring on an asthma attack. The band is bringing out a new album. That song brings back memories of my first job. The new government promised to bring down unemployment. She fainted, but a glass of water soon brought her round.

L.p: *Take after* = look or behave like an older relative; *take back* = withdraw what you said; *take in* = understand, or deceive; *take off* = leave the ground, start to improve, or imitate; *take on* = employ, or accept; *take over* = start doing a job; *take to* = start to like; *take up* = start a hobby.

L.e: Lucy takes after her mum – they both love music. I'm sorry; I take back what I said. The lecture was so fast that I couldn't take it all in. The plane took off on time. The company is taking on new staff. Who will take over when the manager retires? I took to my new neighbours immediately. My dad took up painting when he retired.

L.e: The investigation brought several new facts to light. The argument came to a head at the board meeting. Don't let people take advantage of your kindness. Children often take their parents for granted. When you plan a trip, take the weather into account. She takes great pride in her garden.

units.sub: get down to, get over, get your own back

L.p: *Get* is very common in spoken English. Its basic meanings are: receive, obtain or buy (I got a text from John. She got top marks); change position or move (How are you getting home?); and change state, become (She's getting better).

L.e: Can you get the door? (answer) I didn't get the joke. (understand) His constant whistling really gets me. (annoys) Did you get to see the castle? (manage) It takes time to get to know a new city.

L.p: *Get across* = communicate an idea; *get at* = reach, find; *get behind with* = fail to do something on time; *get down* = make depressed; *get down to* = start giving serious attention to; *get into* = be accepted (by a college); *get on* = manage, or make progress; *get out of* = avoid a responsibility; *get over* = recover from; *get round* = spread; *get round to* = finally do something you intended; *get through* = finish successfully, or use up; *get up to* = do (often something bad).

L.h: A Phrasal verbs based on set

L.p: *Set aside* = reserve (money), or ignore (feelings); *set off* = begin a journey, or cause (an avalanche); *set out* = begin something with a particular aim; *set up* = establish (a business).

L.e: Every month Clare sets aside a little money for travel. Last spring she finally set off for South America. She had set out to visit ten countries in six months, and on her return she set up a small travel blog.

L.p: *Put forward* = propose; *put in* = submit (a form), say (a remark) or install (heating); *put across* = communicate; *put down* = make someone look small; *put together* = assemble; *put on* = present (a play) or pretend to have (an accent); *put out* = inconvenience; *put away* = tidy; *put up* = give someone a place to stay, raise (prices) or display (posters); *put off* = postpone, or distract; *put up with* = tolerate.

L.e: Our neighbour put forward a plan to clean up the park. He's great at putting his ideas across. We spent all afternoon putting together a new bookcase. The drama club is putting on a musical in May. Could you put me up for a night when I'm in town? The meeting has been put off until next week. The smell of the fish put me off my dinner. I don't know how you put up with that noise.

His rude remarks really put my back up.

L.h: A Phrasal verbs based on come

L.p: *Come off* = take place, succeed; *come out* = be published; *come up* = be raised; *come round* = visit informally; *come between* = separate, be a barrier between; *come across* = find by chance; *come by* = obtain; *come down* = decrease; *come up with* = think of (a plan).

L.e: The deal we planned never came off. The new album comes out on Friday. A problem came up at work, so I'll be late. Come round for coffee tomorrow. I came across some old letters in the attic. Good jobs are hard to come by these days. She came up with a brilliant plan.

L.h: B Collocations with come to and come into

L.p: *Come to* often means 'arrive at': come to an agreement, a decision, a conclusion, an end, a *standstill* (= stop), *terms with* (= accept psychologically). *Come into* often means starting or getting: come into contact with, a *fortune* (= receive when someone dies), existence, fashion, *operation* (= start working), sight or view.

L.e: After the accident, traffic on the motorway came to a standstill. It took her years to come to terms with her father's death. When her grandfather died, she came into a fortune. The new tram line will come into operation next year. As we drove round the bend, the castle came into view.

L.h: C Phrasal verbs based on go

L.p: *Go on* = happen, continue, pass (time), go ahead, or criticise (He's always going on at me). *Go through* = experience, check, or be completed (The deal didn't go through). *Go for* = attack, or choose. *Go with* = match.

L.e: They opened a bakery and really made a go of it. I've been on the go since six this morning. It goes without saying that you're welcome to stay. Fans went to great lengths to get tickets. After two bad years, the airline went bankrupt.

L.e: The council is looking into complaints about noise. I know the weather is bad, but look on the bright side – we've got the whole day together.

He turned down the job because it meant moving abroad. Only six people turned up to the meeting. After the party I decided to turn over a new leaf and get fit. The stranger turned out to be my cousin.

L.p: How formal you are depends on who you are talking or writing to, and why. Formal language suits official letters, academic writing and situations where you want to show respect or keep some distance. Informal language suits friends and family and creates a sense of closeness. Mixing the two can sound strange, so choose one style and keep to it.

t: place (informal: Let's go back to my place)

L.h: C Words of Latin and Greek origin

L.p: Many long words from Latin and Greek are formal, and their neutral equivalents are often shorter: *immediately* = at once (informal: right away); *utilise* = use; *occur* = happen; *establish* = show, prove; *provide* = give; *attempt* = try; *seek* = look for; *fundamental* = basic.

Typical of academic and official language: *in terms of* = as regards; *in particular* = especially; *on account of* = because of; *on the basis of* = according to; *in relation to* = about, in connection with.

L.e: The flight was cancelled on account of fog. Places are offered on the basis of exam results. Our town is doing well in terms of jobs, but not in relation to housing.
This entrance is closed until further notice. Passengers should not alight until the train is stationary. Maximum capacity: twelve persons. All purchases must be paid for at the main till.

L.tip: Make sure you could tell a friend what a notice says in everyday words: 'Don't get off the bus while it's moving.'

L.p: *Slang* is very informal vocabulary used mostly among friends. It can make speech lively, but it dates quickly and may offend people, so be careful with it. L.p: A *simile* compares one thing with another using *as … as* or *like*. Most fixed similes belong to relaxed, everyday conversation and can be humorous; a few are unkind about people's looks or abilities, so think before you use them. Picturing the image helps you remember the meaning: *as cool as a cucumber* = very calm.

L.e: Without my glasses I'm as blind as a bat. My grandson is as thin as a rake but as strong as an ox. During the exam the class was as quiet as a mouse. Even under pressure, the pilot stayed as cool as a cucumber. Our new manager is as busy as a bee.

After a month with no rain, the garden was as dry as a bone. The puzzle was as easy as pie. The cat caught the mouse as quick as a flash. When she saw the bill, she went as white as a sheet. He walked into the meeting late, as bold as brass. When they lost the final, the fans were as sick as a parrot. I went as red as a beetroot when I forgot her name. The driver was as sober as a judge.

L.tip: You can also make your own comparison with *as … as can be*: The children were as happy as can be.

L.e: The new software works like a dream. Our teacher has eyes like a hawk – she notices everything. After the long walk I slept like a log. My teenage son eats like a horse. He came into the antique shop like a bull in a china shop. Mentioning taxes to my uncle is like a red rag to a bull.

L.p: Many proverbs feature animals. *When the cat's away, the mice will play* means that people misbehave when nobody is watching them. *You can lead a horse to water, but you can't make it drink* means that you can give someone a chance, but you can't make them take it. *One swallow doesn't make a summer* warns that one good sign is not proof that things have improved.

units.t: The language of signs and notices

L.p: Newspaper *headlines* use as few words as possible. Small words like *the* and *is* are often dropped: TRAIN FARES RISE AGAIN. The present simple describes recent events: TEENAGER WINS CHESS TITLE. *To* + infinitive refers to the future: COUNCIL TO CLOSE LIBRARY.

Many of these words can be nouns or verbs: PM TO CURB SPENDING (limit); BOOK LINKS SPY WITH ENEMY (connects); PM PLEDGES BACKING (promises support). Headlines also use abbreviations: PM (Prime Minister), MP (Member of Parliament). The word *Briton* is almost only found in newspapers.

Some newspapers play with words. SURGICAL CUTS (fewer surgeons: cuts = reductions and a surgeon's cuts). DRAMATIC PAWS (a new production of the musical Cats: paws sounds like pause). HOT HEIR (a prince speaks about climate change: heir sounds like air).

L.p: American English differs from British English most in pronunciation, but also in vocabulary, spelling and some grammar. Americans say *the fall*; British speakers say *autumn*. Americans say *on the weekend*; British English prefers *at the weekend*. Generally, British and American speakers understand each other easily.
American spelling is usually simpler: *-our* → *-or* (colour → color), *-re* → *-er* (centre → center), *-ise* → *-ize* (realise → realize), and jewellery → jewelry.

L.h: C US words and their British equivalents

L.tip: Many words are pronounced differently in American and British English, for example *tomato* and *schedule*. Online dictionaries often let you listen to both versions.

L.p: Some words mean different things in each variety: the British *ground floor* is the American *first floor*, and the British *first floor* is the American *second floor*. British *pants* are underpants; American *pants* are trousers. A British *vest* is an American *undershirt*; an American *vest* is a British *waistcoat*. A British *bill* in a restaurant is an American *check*; an American *bill* is a British *note* (money). In Britain you *wash up* the dishes; in the US you *wash up* your hands.
